extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety/compliance officers, industry stakeholders, and commenters on the OSHA proposed heat standard (NPRM)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the employer obligations and evaluative requirements from OSHA's proposed heat standard (NPRM) covering monitoring, hazard evaluation, employee involvement, drinking water, break areas, acclimatization, rest breaks, communication, and related equipment/frequency expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat monitoring options and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers are required to monitor heat conditions using either local heat index forecasts or on-site measurement of heat index or wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT). Employers with indoor work sites do not have the option of monitoring local weather forecasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes outdoor employers without current monitoring will monitor local forecasts (daily maximum heat index) and may have a designated person at each work site track local ambient temperature and humidity forecasts provided by the NWS (or others). OSHA assumes on average 15 seconds twice a day to monitor the local forecast via a smartphone app. For on-site monitoring, employers may choose between measuring the heat index (measuring ambient temperature and humidity and calculating heat index using OSHA-NIOSH Heat Safety Tool App or NWS online calculator) or measuring WBGT. OSHA estimates measuring the heat index will take the designated person ~1 minute each time, with measurements taken on average twice per work day (260 days/year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring equipment and measurement-method requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may use temperature and humidity loggers capable of automatically uploading relevant environmental information, or purchase WBGT thermometers to measure WBGT on site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes employers using the heat-index measurement approach will use a temperature and humidity logger that can auto-upload data for recordkeeping and that the designated person will spend 15 minutes reading the logger's user manual. For WBGT measurement, employers would need to purchase one WBGT thermometer per worksite and have staff read the thermometer manual; OSHA assumes no new employers will adopt WBGT for this analysis but employers already using it may continue. Table VIII.C.11 lists equipment-based unit costs (e.g., Monitoring Equipment—Indoor unit cost $99.00; Source: Kestrel Instruments, 2024).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard evaluation to identify heat-exposed work areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers with indoor work sites are required to conduct a hazard evaluation to identify the work areas where there is a reasonable expectation that employees are or may be exposed to heat at or above the initial heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimates conducting the hazard evaluation would require about 3 hours in total. Table VIII.C.10 provides labor-based unit costs for identifying heat hazards by industry sector; Table VIII.C.11 shows related equipment costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee input and involvement in evaluations and monitoring plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must seek the input and involvement of non-managerial employees and their representatives, if any, when evaluating the work site to identify work areas with a reasonable expectation of exposures at or above the initial heat trigger and in developing and updating monitoring plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA states that time to develop monitoring plans and employee input is captured within HIIPP development time estimates, but where separately estimated, employee input for evaluating work sites would require 15 minutes per employee providing input; the analysis assumes four employees per establishment would provide input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to forgo measurements by assuming worst-case (both heat triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard allows employers to forgo taking measurements if they assume that a work area meets or exceeds both heat triggers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers electing this option would not incur monitoring costs but would be required to comply with all control measures required at both the initial and high heat triggers as though measurements met or exceeded the high heat trigger. OSHA assumes no employers will newly adopt this option in its baseline cost analysis and welcomes feedback on that assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drinking water provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers would be required to provide access to one quart (32 fluid ounces) of suitably cool drinking water per employee per hour for the entire shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes employers would purchase 40-quart water coolers (with spigots) sufficient to provide the required amount of water and estimates one 40-quart cooler per 40 employees. Employers are assumed to purchase one reusable water bottle per employee. Because existing OSHA standards already require employers to provide drinking water, OSHA assumes nearly all employers currently provide water and incremental costs arise only when the specified quantity is not already provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break area requirements for outdoor worksites
rubrics_metrics.description: For outdoor work sites, employers would be required to provide employees working outdoors with a break area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break areas must be readily accessible to the work area and able to accommodate the number of employees on break; they must have artificial or natural shade or be an air-conditioned space (e.g., trailers, vehicles, structures). OSHA assumes employers without existing break areas will use artificial shade in the form of a 12x12 foot tent that all employees on break can reasonably access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break area and work area controls for indoor worksites
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers with indoor work sites must provide break areas that are readily accessible, able to accommodate employees on break, and that are air-conditioned or have increased air movement and, if appropriate, de-humidification; employers also must provide measures that reduce employee exposure to heat in the work area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One way to comply is by providing increased air movement and, if appropriate, de-humidification. OSHA assumes employers without existing air conditioning/fans/dehumidifiers will (on average) provide two fans per ten employees and, in States where humid conditions may occur, two dehumidifiers per ten employees. Table VIII.C.14 shows equipment costs for water coolers, water bottles, pedestal fans, dehumidifiers, and tents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization protections for new and returning employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must adopt protections for new and returning employees who may not be acclimatized to working in the heat at or above the initial heat trigger during their first week on the job or their first week back after an employee is away from work for more than 14 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For new employees, employers should implement a plan that incorporates measures required in paragraph (f) when the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded during the first week of work. OSHA calculated costs of rest breaks and observation for signs and symptoms during an employee's first week. OSHA assumes the hazard alert can be provided by the designated person while conducting observation or during training. Estimated additional time: ~41.75 minutes/day per new indoor employee and ~47.75 minutes/day per new outdoor employee during the first week (for 8-hour shifts when initial but not high heat trigger is met). OSHA solicits comment on whether reduced pacing during acclimatization could yield cost savings that should offset these costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid if-needed rest breaks at the initial heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: When the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded, employers must allow and encourage employees to take paid rest breaks if needed to prevent overheating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes at-risk employees will take one 10-minute if-needed rest break per 8-hour shift; additional walking time assumed is 2 minutes for indoor employees and 4 minutes for outdoor employees per break. OSHA preliminarily determined that offering rest breaks yields employer cost savings due to reduced pacing (increased efficiency during work time), and quantifies such savings by defining three employee groups (Group 1: no current rest breaks; Group 2: currently provide if-needed breaks at initial trigger only; Group 3: provide rest breaks meeting initial and high triggers) and estimating pacing minutes and reductions (see Table VIII.C.12). OSHA welcomes feedback on the assumption that an average employee will take one 10-minute if-needed rest break and on travel time assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective two-way communication requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers would be required to maintain a means of effective two-way communication with employees whenever the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes a designated person would communicate with each employee three times for every 8-hour shift that meets or exceeds the initial heat trigger, spending 15 seconds on each communication. At-risk workers are assumed to spend the same amount of time communicating with the designated person. OSHA assumes employers and employees have current methods for two-way communication (e.g., cell phones, walkie-talkies) that may be used for these communications. Table VIII.C.13 and subsequent rows list unit costs (supervisor and employee time) by sector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and recurrence expectations for monitoring and evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard specifies frequencies for several activities: monitoring frequency, frequency of measurements, hazard-identification periodicity, and one-time review obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the analysis: OSHA assumes monitoring (forecast checks or heat-index measurements) will be done on average twice per work day; designated person reading logger manual is a one-time task (assumed 15 minutes); indoor identification of heat-exposed work areas is estimated every 5 years; measurement-based activities are typically estimated on a daily basis when triggers are met. The labor/equipment tables provide sector-specific hour/frequency bases (e.g., 'Establishment Annual', 'Every 5 Years', 'One-Time', 'Daily at Initial Heat Trigger (Up to 5 Days)').
